title: Learning Dynamics Features via Policy Attention for Path Planning
one_liner: A framework that filters global traffic information down to just the most important parts for learning which road to take.
lead: When robots or navigation apps plan routes through traffic, they face a tradeoff: use all available information and get bogged down in irrelevant details, or use only nearby information and miss critical context. This paper proposes a method that keeps the best of both worlds by automatically identifying which global traffic patterns actually matter for good decisions.

problem.h2: The roadblock: too much or too little information
paras: Urban traffic changes constantly. A route that was good five minutes ago may now be jammed. An AI system that plans routes needs to adapt in real time — reinforcement learning (learning from experience to make better decisions) lets it do this by observing what happens when it tries different routes, then nudges its choices toward roads that get you there faster.

But here is the trap: to make good decisions, the system needs to know what is happening on the road network. If it looks at ALL traffic data everywhere, it has a complete picture but drowns in noise—processing every traffic camera, every sensor reading, every minor incident, most of which do not affect the route you are planning. That is computationally expensive and slow. If it looks only at nearby traffic, it runs fast, but it might miss that a major highway ahead is completely blocked.

A naive approach fails because no single choice works: global data guarantees you see everything that matters, but wastes energy on everything that does not; local data is efficient but blindsided by distant obstacles.

callout.html: How do you automatically decide which pieces of global traffic information actually matter for planning this specific route?

panels.title: 1. All traffic data
panels.caption: Global traffic map: most sensors irrelevant, a few critical ones.

panels.title: 2. Naive local lookup
panels.caption: Using only nearby data: fast but misses distant blockages ahead.

panels.title: 3. Policy filters by importance
panels.caption: Scoring mechanism picks top-k shortest paths that matter for this decision.

panels.title: 4. Refinement by neighborhood
panels.caption: Expand selected paths to nearby neighborhoods for local context.

panels.title: 5. Compact feature set
panels.caption: Learned model trains on distilled features: complete enough, fast enough.

steps.text: Read the current state of every road, signal, and incident in the network.
Compute the k shortest paths from origin to destination using classical routing.
For each selected path, collect traffic data from roads within n hops of that path.
Pack the selected and neighboring data into a compact list of numbers for the learner.
Feed these compact features to a reinforcement learning model, which learns to choose routes that arrive on time.

paras: The paper changes how the reinforcement learning system represents traffic information — what it actually sees and thinks about when making a routing decision. Instead of a sprawling global snapshot or a myopic local view, it builds a custom feature representation (a compact list of numbers) that contains exactly the information relevant to each route-planning decision.

hidden.name: state completeness
paras: Information sufficiency is the degree to which a representation contains enough signal to make an optimal decision. If you throw away a road's traffic data, can you still find the best route? This paper calls this quantity state completeness: a measure of whether the compressed feature set still preserves enough information to guarantee a route planner can learn the right choice.

The paper proves mathematically that the DFR (Dynamics Feature Representation) method guarantees state completeness, meaning the compact features you extract from the top-k paths and their neighborhoods contain sufficient information to find near-optimal routes. This is the key hidden quantity — without it, you are flying blind and might inadvertently omit critical data.

heat.caption: Darker means more critical to ensuring the model sees enough information to make good decisions.

reads.html: State completeness means: did you leave out any information that would change the right answer? The paper shows that by selecting top-k paths and their neighborhoods, you keep enough signal.

Theoretical analysis of state completeness: extracting paths within n hops of the top-k shortest paths forms a sufficient state representation for near-optimal policy learning in the MDP (Markov decision process) defined by dynamic routing.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: the filtering chain
paras: The trick is to ask: which parts of the global traffic map actually influence what I decide right now? The answer is the set of possible routes I might take. If I compute the k shortest paths from here to the destination, those paths represent the routes my decision-making algorithm is most likely to explore. Any traffic data far from these paths is unlikely to shift my choice.

Once you know which paths matter, you can expand each path to include nearby roads (within n hops), because traffic on a neighboring street might cause a jam that forces a detour. This expansion anchors the feature set to real geography, not abstract paths. The result is a feature vector that is much smaller than the global state, but large enough to contain all the information needed to learn which route works best.

Why does this make learning faster and more accurate? Because the learned model (the reinforcement learning agent) no longer wastes neurons on irrelevant roads and sensors. It focuses on the roads that actually affect its choices. Training converges faster because the signal-to-noise ratio is higher: every number in the feature vector changes in ways that matter to the decision, not buried in noise from distant, irrelevant parts of the network.

stages.s: Full traffic snapshot: all roads, all sensors, all incidents
Rank all paths by distance; keep top k
For each path, gather data from neighboring roads within n hops
Feed to reinforcement learning model to train route choice

math.words: The feature vector is built by: (1) computing the set of top-k shortest paths, (2) for each path, collecting all traffic data on that path and within n hops, (3) concatenating into one vector. The value of information sufficiency is guaranteed by the fact that these paths and neighborhoods cover all roads that could affect the optimal decision.
math.equation: feat = concat( traffic( union( n_hop_neighborhood(P_i) for i in top_k_paths() ) ) )
symbols: the k shortest paths from origin to destination
all roads within n steps of path P_i
the current traffic state of each road
stack all values into one feature vector
the compact feature representation fed to the learner

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose we have 100 roads in the network and compute top-3 shortest paths.
Path 1 has 20 roads; its 2-hop neighborhood adds 15 more. Total: 35 roads.
Path 2 has 18 roads; its neighborhood adds 12. Total: 30 roads.
Path 3 has 19 roads; its neighborhood adds 14. Total: 33 roads.
Union of all three: 35 + 30 + 33 - (overlaps) = roughly 50 unique roads covered.
Feature vector size: 50 traffic readings, instead of 100. Compression 2x; computation cut in half.
Guaranteed: those 50 roads include every decision point that affects the route choice.

math.note: The feature vector is a compact projection of global data, built by following the shortest paths the agent might explore.

charts.title: Classical routing (no learning)
charts.note: Routes do not adapt to real-time traffic changes; frozen after computation.

charts.title: Naive RL (all global data)
charts.note: Learns good routes but training is slow because the model processes irrelevant information.

charts.title: DFR (this paper)
charts.note: Trains faster because the model no longer wastes computation on irrelevant roads; finds better routes because it can now focus on data that actually changes decisions; uses less memory because the feature set is smaller, which lets the model fit more patterns with fewer numbers.

items.html: If you keep only 2 or 3 shortest paths, you might miss the actual best route when traffic conditions are unusual. The top-k cutoff must be large enough that the real optimal path falls within the k shortest in typical conditions.

If neighborhoods are only 1 hop away, you miss traffic on streets just beyond the immediate perimeter. A jam one block away might not show up, and the model will learn routes that look good locally but fail globally.

items.b: Sudden major incidents far from selected paths.
items.html: If a major highway fails or a new bridge opens outside the top-k paths and their neighborhoods, the model does not see it and cannot adapt. The method assumes the best routes do not deviate drastically from classical shortest-path rankings.

items.b: Done right: adaptive k and n.
items.html: Choose k and n large enough to cover the decision space under normal conditions, but no larger. Monitor model performance in the real world and increase k or n if a pattern of missed opportunities emerges.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simulation of a small urban network (say, 50 streets, 1 origin, 1 destination). Simulate time-varying traffic (congestion appears at different times on different roads). Train a standard reinforcement learning agent (1) on the full global traffic state, (2) on only local 1-hop neighbors, and (3) on the DFR features from top-3 paths and 2-hop neighborhoods. Measure three metrics for each: training time (wall-clock seconds per episode), final route quality (average time to reach destination after training), and memory use (bytes of the learned model). The demo should show that DFR achieves comparable or better route quality to full global data, because the filtered features still contain all the roads that appear in possible routes, so the model learns the same decision-making rules but with 3x to 5x lower training time and memory use, since it processes fewer irrelevant numbers.
demo.metric_eq: improvement = (time_naive_rl - time_DFR) / time_naive_rl ; likewise for memory_usage ; route_quality measured as mean travel time after convergence
demo.closing: The demo must make it impossible to miss the core tradeoff: global data is complete but slow; local data is fast but incomplete; DFR extracts the minimal sufficient information to get the speed of local data with the completeness of global data.
